title: Key mappings don't work when Visual Studio has focus

judgment.rationale: The original repro is clear but old: CapsLock/Ctrl and Win/Alt remaps work outside Visual Studio and revert inside it. A commenter points out that an elevated Visual Studio requires PowerToys at the same elevation, but the original report does not establish Visual Studio's elevation state.
evidence: The reporter used PowerToys 0.66.0 on Windows 10 and says the remaps work until Visual Studio 2022 is focused.
A second reporter describes similar behavior in Visual Studio 2022 on Windows 10 with PowerToys 0.74.1.
A later commenter notes that if Visual Studio runs as administrator, PowerToys must also run as administrator; no confirmation of the original VS elevation state is present.
judgment.recommended_action: Reproduce the remap in Visual Studio at matching and mismatched integrity levels before treating this as an application-specific interception defect.

fix_assessment.rationale: The existing discussion identifies an elevation boundary as a plausible explanation, but no current matched-elevation reproduction establishes a PowerToys defect.

issue_context.summary: CapsLock/Ctrl and Win/Alt remaps reportedly stop applying while Visual Studio is focused; process elevation is an unresolved discriminator.
known_information: The original report uses PowerToys 0.66.0, Visual Studio Community 2022, and Windows 10 21H2; PowerToys itself was not running as administrator.
A later report describes similar behavior in VS 2022 Enterprise on Windows 10 Enterprise with PowerToys 0.74.1.
A commenter advises matching PowerToys elevation to an elevated Visual Studio process.
The original reporter observes remapping resumes when focus leaves Visual Studio.
inferences: A UIPI/integrity-level boundary could explain why a non-elevated PowerToys hook cannot affect an elevated Visual Studio window.
If the behavior persists at matching elevation, a Visual Studio-specific focus or hook issue remains possible.
issue_context.analysis: A useful maintainer check is a four-cell elevation comparison with a simple remap. This can separate a known Windows privilege boundary from an application-specific Keyboard Manager regression without requesting broad logs.
initial_investigation: Read the full issue body and all three comments.
The discussion includes a direct elevation explanation but no confirmation of the app's elevation state or current build.

actions.label: Compare Visual Studio and PowerToys elevation

reproduce.title: Test keyboard remapping across Visual Studio integrity levels
prerequisites: Visual Studio 2022 on Windows 10 or Windows 11.
A clean profile with one simple key remap, such as CapsLock to Ctrl.
steps: Test the remap in a standard unelevated text editor.
Run both PowerToys and Visual Studio unelevated and test the remap in a Visual Studio editor.
Run Visual Studio elevated while PowerToys remains unelevated and repeat.
Run both elevated and repeat; compare the four results and confirm remapping returns after leaving Visual Studio.
reproduce.expected_result: Remapping works when PowerToys and the target process have compatible integrity levels; any failure at matching levels identifies a separate regression.
